The Case for Complete Deregulation of Pornography

It asks judges and juries to determine the aesthetic and moral worth of expression, precisely the task the First Amendment was designed to remove from government hands.

The line between "erotica" and "pornography"—between protected and unprotected—has always been drawn by those in power against those they disdained.

John Stuart Mill's marketplace of ideas remains our best framework for understanding free speech. Mill argued that suppressing any opinion—even one universally considered false or harmful—damages society by eliminating the possibility of exchanging error for truth or clarifying partial truths. This principle applies equally to all forms of expression, including sexual content.

Current obscenity laws create numerous practical problems that demonstrate the impossibility of coherent enforcement:

  2. Technological Reality: The internet has made geographic boundaries largely meaningless for content distribution. Attempting to enforce local community standards on globally accessible content is both practically impossible and constitutionally suspect.

  3. Selective Enforcement: Obscenity prosecutions often reflect the political priorities of prosecutors rather than consistent application of law, raising equal protection concerns.

Advocating for deregulation of adult content does not mean abandoning all legal standards. Clear distinctions exist between content regulation and conduct regulation:

  • Child Protection: Laws protecting minors from exploitation are conduct regulations that address actual harm, not speech restrictions.
  • Consent: Requirements that all participants be consenting adults address conduct, not expression.
  • Privacy: Laws protecting against non-consensual distribution of intimate images protect individual privacy rights.
  • Commercial Fraud: Truth-in-advertising laws apply neutrally to all commerce.

These regulations target harmful conduct while remaining content-neutral, unlike obscenity laws that criminalize expression based on its message.

The Benefits of Deregulation

Complete deregulation would produce several positive outcomes:

  1. Legal Clarity: Eliminating vague obscenity standards would provide clear guidance for content creators and platforms.

  2. Reduced Incarceration: Ending obscenity prosecutions would reduce prison populations and associated costs.

The Case for Abolishing Obscenity Laws: Free Expression Without Asterisks

An Argument for Ending Government Regulation of Pornographic Content Among Consenting Adults

Introduction

Few areas of law reveal the contradictions in a society's commitment to free expression more starkly than obscenity regulation. The United States, along with most liberal democracies, professes a foundational commitment to freedom of speech and expression—then carves out an unprincipled exception for sexual content that offends majoritarian sensibilities. Obscenity laws are not relics of a forgotten past; they remain enforceable federal and state statutes, weaponized selectively by prosecutors and subject to standards so vague they would be struck down instantly in any other area of First Amendment jurisprudence. The time has come to acknowledge what decades of legal scholarship, philosophical argument, and practical experience have demonstrated: all obscenity laws governing expression between and by consenting adults should be abolished, and pornographic content should receive the same constitutional protection as political pamphlets, violent films, and religious screeds.

This is not a marginal or frivolous argument. It follows directly from principles that most citizens and legal scholars already accept in every other context. If free speech means anything, it must mean that the government cannot criminalize expression simply because a majority of people find it distasteful, offensive, or morally objectionable.

I. The Incoherence of Obscenity Doctrine

Any serious argument for deregulation must begin with the bankruptcy of existing obscenity law. In Miller v. California (1973), the Supreme Court established a three-pronged test for obscenity: (1) whether the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find that the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest; (2) whether the work depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way; and (3) whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

Each prong is a study in constitutional dysfunction.

Community standards are inherently arbitrary. The Miller test openly acknowledges that identical content can be legally protected in San Francisco and criminal in rural Mississippi. No other category of speech is subject to such geographic relativism. We do not permit communities to ban political speech they find offensive, nor do we allow local majorities to outlaw religious expression that violates prevailing norms. The notion that constitutional protection should depend on the moral sensibilities of one's neighbors is antithetical to the very purpose of the Bill of Rights, which exists precisely to protect individuals and minorities against majoritarian overreach.

"Patent offensiveness" is pure subjectivity. The Court has never provided a workable definition of what makes a depiction of sex "patently offensive" as opposed to merely explicit. This is not a gap that further jurisprudence can fill; it is a structural defect. Offensiveness is a reaction, not a property of content. The same material that disgusts one viewer arouses another, bores a third, and strikes a fourth as artistically meaningful. Criminalizing content based on the emotional reaction it produces in a hypothetical "average person" is indistinguishable from criminalizing content based on its unpopularity—precisely what the First Amendment forbids.

The "serious value" test empowers judges as art critics. Under Miller's third prong, a work escapes criminal prosecution only if a court determines it has "serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value." This hands the judiciary the power to determine what counts as art—a role that courts are spectacularly ill-equipped to perform and that the Constitution never assigned them. The history of censorship is a graveyard of works initially denied value and later recognized as significant: Ulysses, Lady Chatterley's Lover, Howl, and countless others. The third prong of Miller is nothing more than a sophistication test, protecting the erotica of the educated classes while leaving vulnerable the sexual expression of those whose tastes are less refined or more direct.

Legal scholars across the ideological spectrum have criticized Miller as one of the worst-reasoned doctrines in First Amendment law. As the late Justice William Brennan—who originally authored the Court's first obscenity framework in Roth v. United States—eventually conceded in his dissent in Paris Adult Theatre I v. Slaton (1973), he had come to believe that the obscenity exception was unworkable and that the Court should abandon the effort to distinguish protected sexual expression from unprotected obscenity. If the architect of modern obscenity doctrine could not sustain faith in its coherence, we should not pretend the doctrine rests on any principled foundation.

II. The First Amendment Admits No Offense-Based Exceptions

The deeper argument against obscenity law is not merely that Miller is poorly designed but that the entire project of criminalizing offensive sexual expression is incompatible with the philosophy underlying free speech.

The First Amendment's purpose is not to protect speech that everyone finds agreeable. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote, "If there is any principle of the Constitution that more imperatively calls for attachment than any other, it is the principle of free thought—not free thought for those who agree with us but freedom for the thought that we hate." The Supreme Court has upheld this principle with remarkable consistency in every domain except sex:

  • Hate speech is constitutionally protected. In Matal v. Tam (2017), the Court unanimously struck down a law banning "disparaging" trademarks, reaffirming that "speech may not be banned on the ground that it expresses ideas that offend."
  • Violent content is constitutionally protected. In Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011), the Court struck down a California law restricting the sale of violent video games to minors, holding that violence—no matter how graphic—does not fall outside the First Amendment.
  • Flag burning is constitutionally protected (Texas v. Johnson, 1989).
  • Funeral protests are constitutionally protected (Snyder v. Phelps, 2011).
  • Depictions of animal cruelty received constitutional protection when the Court struck down the Crush Video Act as overbroad (United States v. Stevens, 2010).

The pattern is unmistakable: the Court has refused, again and again, to allow the government to suppress expression merely because it is offensive, disturbing, or morally repugnant—except when that expression involves sex. The obscenity exception is the last surviving offense-based restriction on expression in American law, and it survives not on principled grounds but on cultural squeamishness and historical inertia.

Why should depictions of sex receive less protection than depictions of murder, torture, or racial hatred? No one has ever provided a satisfying answer. The standard response—that obscenity has traditionally been unprotected—is an appeal to history that proves nothing about constitutional principle. Seditious libel was also traditionally unprotected, as was blasphemy. Traditions of censorship are not self-justifying; they are the very thing the First Amendment was designed to challenge.

III. The Harm Argument Does Not Survive Scrutiny

Defenders of obscenity law frequently argue that pornography causes tangible harm—to women, to children, to relationships, to the social fabric—and that these harms justify regulation. This argument fails on multiple levels.

The empirical evidence is contested and inconclusive. Decades of social science research have failed to establish a clear causal link between consumption of pornography and sexual violence. Multiple countries that have liberalized pornography laws—including Denmark, Japan, and the Czech Republic—have experienced declining rates of sexual assault. While correlation does not prove causation, these data at minimum undercut the claim that pornography availability increases sexual violence. The most comprehensive meta-analyses find modest correlational effects on attitudes but no consistent evidence of behavioral harm that would justify criminal prohibition.

Even if some pornography influences attitudes, that is not sufficient grounds for prohibition. It is well-established that political propaganda, religious extremism, and media depictions of violence also influence attitudes and behavior. We do not criminalize these forms of expression on the basis of their possible attitudinal effects because doing so would annihilate the First Amendment. The remedy for potentially harmful speech is counter-speech, education, and cultural engagement—not the prison cell.

The harm argument often conflates distinct issues. Many of the genuine harms associated with the pornography industry—coercion, trafficking, exploitation, abuse of performers—are already addressed by existing criminal law. Assault is a crime. Trafficking is a crime. Coercion is a crime. Fraud is a crime. Production involving minors is a crime, and nothing in the argument for abolishing obscenity laws touches the overwhelming consensus that the sexual exploitation of children must remain criminally prohibited. The appropriate response to criminal conduct within an industry is to prosecute the criminal conduct, not to ban the industry's expressive output. We do not ban journalism because some journalists commit fraud; we do not ban filmmaking because some producers engage in abuse.

The "harm to the viewer" rationale is paternalism, not liberalism. If the state can restrict access to pornography because viewing it is harmful to the viewer, then the state can restrict access to alcohol, fast food, gambling, extreme sports, or any other activity that may negatively affect those who choose to engage in it. A free society trusts adults to make their own choices about what to view, read, and think—even when those choices are unwise.

IV. Content Regulation Is the Tool of Authoritarianism

History provides an unambiguous lesson: obscenity laws are instruments of power, wielded against the marginalized and the dissident far more often than against genuine exploiters.

Obscenity prosecutions have historically targeted:

  • LGBTQ+ expression. For most of the twentieth century, any positive depiction of homosexuality was treated as obscene per se. Magazines, novels, and films depicting same-sex relationships were seized, banned, and prosecuted. The conflation of queerness with obscenity was not an incidental misapplication of the law; it was the law's intended function.
  • Feminist and reproductive health literature. Under the Comstock laws—the ancestors of modern obscenity statutes—information about contraception and reproductive health was classified as obscene. Margaret Sanger was prosecuted for distributing pamphlets about birth control.
  • Avant-garde art and literature. As noted above, works by James Joyce, D.H. Lawrence, Allen Ginsberg, Henry Miller, and many others were subjected to obscenity prosecution.
  • Marginalized communities. Enforcement has consistently fallen hardest on those with the least social and political power—sex workers, racial minorities, the poor—while the erotica consumed by affluent, educated, white audiences has gone largely unmolested.

This pattern is not accidental. Obscenity law, by its very nature, grants the state discretionary power to suppress sexual expression based on vaguely defined community standards. Discretionary power will always be exercised disproportionately against the vulnerable and the unpopular. Abolishing obscenity law does not merely remove a theoretical risk of abuse; it eliminates a tool that has been used for over a century to persecute minorities and suppress dissent.

V. The Digital Age Has Made Obscenity Regulation Functionally Absurd

Even setting aside the principled arguments, obscenity enforcement has become practically untenable. The internet has made pornographic content universally accessible. Community standards in pornography consumption are effectively national and global; the notion that a community can insulate itself from sexual content that its members choose to access is a fiction. Attempting to enforce obscenity laws in the digital age means either engaging in mass surveillance of internet activity—a civil liberties catastrophe—or selectively prosecuting a handful of producers and distributors to "send a message," which amounts to the arbitrary exercise of prosecutorial power against a few while the underlying conduct remains universal.

The resources spent on obscenity enforcement would be far better directed toward combating actual exploitation, supporting trafficking victims, and prosecuting those who produce content through force, fraud, or coercion.

VI. Moral Disapproval Is Not a Legitimate Basis for Criminal Law

At its root, obscenity regulation rests on the premise that the state may criminalize expression because it is morally offensive. This premise is flatly incompatible with liberalism. As John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty, "The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not sufficient warrant."

The Supreme Court itself has increasingly moved toward this position in other domains. In Lawrence v. Texas (2003), the Court struck down sodomy laws, holding that moral disapproval of a practice is not a legitimate state interest sufficient to justify criminal prohibition. In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), the Court extended constitutional protection to same-sex marriage. The logic of these decisions is incompatible with the continued criminalization of sexual expression between consenting adults. If the state cannot criminalize private sexual conduct based on moral disapproval, it should not be able to criminalize depictions of that conduct on the same basis.

VII. The Path Forward

Abolishing obscenity laws does not mean abandoning all regulation of sexually explicit industries. A deregulated framework would still include:

  • Absolute prohibition on the sexual exploitation of minors. This is not an obscenity issue; it is a child protection issue, and it is grounded in the prevention of direct, concrete harm to real victims.
  • Enforcement of laws against coercion, trafficking, fraud, and assault within the production of pornographic content.
  • Workplace safety regulations for performers, as in any other industry.
  • Robust age-verification mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing commercial pornographic content—mechanisms designed with both child safety and privacy in mind.
  • Consumer protection and transparency requirements for the industry.

What would be eliminated is the government's power to criminalize the content itself—to imprison people for creating, distributing, or possessing expression that the state deems insufficiently valuable or excessively sexual. This power has no place in a free society.

Conclusion

The argument for abolishing obscenity laws is not a defense of pornography as such. One need not enjoy, approve of, or consume pornography to recognize that the government has no business deciding what sexual content adults may create, share, and view. Obscenity law is intellectually incoherent, historically abusive, practically unenforceable, and philosophically incompatible with the principles of free expression and individual liberty that supposedly define liberal democracy.

Every argument marshaled in defense of obscenity regulation—community standards, moral harm, social fabric, public decency—has been deployed throughout history to suppress political dissent, persecute minorities, and control the bodies and desires of the powerless. Every time we have examined these arguments in other contexts, we have found them wanting and have chosen liberty over paternalism. The same choice awaits us here.

Free speech is not a principle that applies only to expression we find palatable. It is a principle that applies most urgently to expression we find disturbing, distasteful, and even repugnant. If we do not extend its protection to the speech we despise, we do not believe in it at all.

The obscenity exception should be closed—permanently, completely, and without apology.
